Fact Sheet for NPDES Permit Renewal, Urbana Wastewater Treatment Plant, 2015
Page 15 of28
Outfall Signage
Part II of the permit includes requirements for the permittee to place and maintain a sign at each outfall to the 
Mad River providing information about the discharge. Signage at outfalls is required pursuant to OAC 3745-33- 
08(A).
Storm Water Compliance
Parts IV, V, and VI have been included with the draft permit to ensure that any storm water flows from the 
facility site are properly regulated and managed. As an alternative to complying with Parts fV, V, and VI, the 
City may seek permit coverage under the general permit for industrial storm water (permit number OHR000005) 
or submit a “No Exposure Certification.” Parts IV, V, and VI will be removed from the final permit if: 1) the 
Urbana submits a Notice of Intent (NOI) for coverage under the general permit for industrial storm water or 
submits a No Exposure Certification, 2) Ohio EPA determines that the facility is eligible for coverage under the 
general permit or meets the requirements for a No Exposure Certification, and 3) the determination by Ohio 
EPA can be made prior to the issuance of the final permit.

V. Pretreatment Program Requirements

3. Industrial User Inventory
The permittee's pretreatment program initially approved February, 1987 and all 
subsequent modifications approved before the effective date of this permit, shall be an 
enforceable term and condition of this permit.
To ensure that the approved program is implemented in accordance with 40 CFR 403, 
Chapter 3745-3 of Ohio Administrative Code and Chapter 6111 of the Ohio Revised 
Code, the peiTnittee shall comply with the following conditions:
The permittee shall adopt and maintain legal authority which enables it to fully 
implement and enforce all aspects of its approved pretreatment program including the 
identification and characterization of industrial sources, issuance of control documents, 
compliance monitoring and reporting, and enforcement.
The permittee shall have sufficient resources and qualified personnel to fully implement 
all aspects of its approved pretreatment program.
The permittee shall establish agreements with all contributing jurisdictions, as necessary, 
to enable the pennittee to fulfill its requirements with respect to industrial users 
discharging to its system.
The permittee shall identify all industrial users subject to pretreatment standards and 
requirements and characterize the nature and volume of pollutants in their wastewater. 
Dischargers determined to be Significant Industrial Users according to OAC 
3745-3-01(FF) must be notified of applicable pretreatment standards and requirements 
within 30 days of making such a determination. This inventory shall be updated at a 
frequency to ensure proper identification and characterization of industrial users.

Dear Mayor and Council:

In order to determine NPDES permit limits that are protective of water quality in the Mad River, 
a Waste Load Allocation was performed. This review looks at existing permit limits and new 
waste load allocation limits to determine acceptable permit limits based upon the proposed 
design flow (4.5 MGD). The tables below contain the draft waste load allocation permit limits, 
and a draft final table with no load increase. The second table, which has no load increase, 
would not require a full anti-degradation review. Either table can be used as a basis for plant 
design. Please be advised draft limits are good for a period of one year from the date of this 
letter.
I am writing in follow-up to your proposed expansion of design flow at the waste water treatment 
plant. This expansion would increase the treatment systems design capacity from 3.0 MGD to 
4.5 MGD. The city currently holds National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) 
permit number 1PD00011*ND for this discharge. The system discharges to the Mad River.

1) eDMR users should select the "No Discharge" check box on the data entry form. PIN the eDMR.
2) Permittees reporting on paper should report "AL" in the first column of the first day of the 4500 Form. Sign the form.
- Units of mg/kg are on a dry weight basis.
- Monitoring is required when sewage sludge is removed from the permittee’s facility for application to the land. The monitoring data shall be 
reported on the December Discharge Monitoring Report (DMR). The monitoring data can be collected at any time during the reporting period.
- Metal pollutant analysis must be completed during each reporting period, whether sewage sludge is removed from the facility or not, or the 
number of composite samples collected and reported shall be increased prior to the next land application event to account for the reporting 
period(s) in which land application did not occur, unless all previously accumulated sewage sludge has been removed and disposed of via a 
landfill, through incineration or by transfer to another treatment works.
- If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period, enter the results for the metal analysis in eDMR or on the 4500 
report and enter “0” for sludge weight and sludge fee weight.
- If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period and no metal analysis is completed during the reporting period, 
the permittee shall report under station 581 in the following manner:
- If metal analysis has not been completed previously during each reporting period: when sewage sludge is removed from the facility all metal 
analysis results shall be reported on the applicable DMR by entering the separate results on different days within the DMR. For example, if no 
sewage sludge has been removed from the facility for a full calendar year, and quarterly monitoring is required by the permit, then five (four 
from the previous year and one for the current monitoring period) separate composite samples of the sewage sludge are required to be 
collected and analyzed for metals prior to removal from the facility. The first sample result may be entered on the first day of the DMR, the 
second result on the second day of the DMR, and so on. A note may then be added to indicate the actual day(s) when the samples were 
collected.
- It is recommended that composite samples of the sewage sludge be collected and analyzed close enough to the time of land application to be 
reflective of the sludge’s current quality, but not so close that the results of the analysis are not available prior to land applying the sludge.
- The permittee shall maintain the appropriate records on site to verify that the requirements of Pathogen Reduction and Vector Attraction 
Reduction have been met.
- Sludge weight is a calculated total for the year. To convert from gallons of liquid sewage sludge to dry tons of sewage sludge: dry tons= 
gallons X 8.34 (Ibs/gallon) x 0.0005 (tons/lb) x decimal fraction total solids.

The permittee shall annually monitor priority pollutants, as defined by U.S. EPA, in the

are occurring at normal to maximum levels. Sampling of the influent shall be done prior 
to any recycle streams and sampling of the effluent shall be after disinfection. Both 
samples shall be collected on the same day or, alternately, the effluent sample may be 
collected following the influent sample by approximately the retention time of the POTW.

minimum of one grab sample shall be taken during actual sludge removal and disposal 
unless the POTW uses more than one disposal option. If multiple disposal options are 
used, the POTW shall collect a composite of grab samples from all disposal practices 
which are proportional to the annual flows to each type of disposal.

(excluding priority pollutants and unsubstituted aliphatic compounds) at each sample 
location. Identification of additional peaks more than ten times higher than the adjacent 
background noise on the total ion plots (reconstructed gas chromatograms) shall be 
attempted through the use of U.S. EPA/NIH computerized library of mass spectra, with 
visual confirmation by an experienced analyst. Quantification may be based on an order 
of magnitude estimate compared with an internal standard.

PART in - GENERAL CONDITIONS
1. DEFINITIONS
"Daily discharge" means the discharge of a pollutant measured during a calendar day or any 24-hour 
period that reasonably represents the calendar day for purposes of sampling. For pollutants with 
limitations expressed in units of mass, the "daily discharge" is calculated as the total mass of the pollutant 
discharged over the day. For pollutants with limitations expressed in other units of measurement, the 
"daily discharge" is calculated as the average measurement of the pollutant over the day.
"Average weekly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar week, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar week divided 
by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that week. Each of the following 7-day periods is 
defined as a calendar week: Week 1 is Days 1 - 7 of the month; Week 2 is Days 8-14; Week 3 is Days 
15-21; and Week 4 is Days 22 - 28. If the "daily discharge" on days 29, 30 or 31 exceeds the "average 
weekly" discharge limitation, Ohio EPA may elect to evaluate the last 7 days of the month as Week 4 
instead of Days 22 - 28. Compliance with fecal coliform bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be 
determined using the geometric mean.
"Average monthly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar month, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar month 
divided by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that month. Compliance with fecal 
coliform bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be determined using the geometric mean.
"85 percent removal" means the arithmetic mean of the values for effluent samples collected in a period 
of 30 consecutive days shall not exceed 15 percent of the arithmetic mean of the values for influent 
samples collected at approximately the same times during the same period.
"Absolute Limitations" Compliance with limitations having descriptions of "shall not be less than," "nor 
greater than," "shall not exceed," "minimum," or "maximum" shall be determined from any single value 
for effluent samples and/or measurements collected.
"Net concentration" shall mean the difference between the concentration of a given substance in a sample 
taken of the discharge and the concentration of the same substances in a sample taken at the intake which 
suppUes water to the given process. For the purpose of this definition, samples that are taken to 
determine the net concentration shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six 
increments taken at regular intervals throughout the plant day.

All wastewater treatment works shall be operated in a manner consistent with the following:
A. In amounts that will settle to form putrescent, or otherwise objectionable, sludge deposits; or that will

nuisance;
D. In amounts that either singly or in combination with other substances are toxic to human, animal, or 
aquatic life;

become inimical to more desirable forms of aquatic life, or create conditions that are unsightly, or 
constitute a nuisance in any other fashion;

all treatment or control facilities or systems installed or used by the permittee necessary to achieve

operation of back-up or auxiliary facilities or similar systems which are installed by a permittee only

"Sewage sludge" means a solid, semi-solid, or liquid residue generated during the treatment of domestic 
sewage in a treatment works as defined in section 6111.01 of the Revised Code. "Sewage sludge" 
includes, but is not limited to, scum or solids removed in primary, secondary, or advanced wastewater 
treatment processes. "Sewage sludge" does not include ash generated during the firing of sewage sludge 
in a sewage sludge incinerator, grit and screenings generated during preliminary treatment of domestic 
sewage in a treatment works, animal manure, residue generated during treatment of animal manure, or 
domestic septage.
"Sewage sludge weight" means the weight of sewage sludge, in dry U.S. tons, including admixtures such 
as liming materials or bulking agents. Monitoring frequencies for sewage sludge parameters are based on 
the reported sludge weight generated in a calendar year (use the most recent calendar year data when the 
NPDES permit is up for renewal).

such as liming materials or bulking agents. Annual sewage sludge fees, as per section 3745.11(Y) of the 
Ohio Revised Code, are based on the reported sludge fee weight for the most recent calendar year.

2) Permittees reporting on paper should report "AL" in the first column of the first day of the 4500 Form. Sign the form.
- Units of mg/kg are on a dry weight basis.
- Monitoring is required when sewage sludge is removed from the permittee’s facility for application to the land. The monitoring data shall be 
reported on the December Discharge Monitoring Report (DMR). The monitoring data can be collected at any time during the reporting period.
- Metal pollutant analysis must be completed during each reporting period, whether sewage sludge is removed from the facility or not, or the 
number of composite samples collected and reported shall be increased prior to the next land application event to account for the reporting 
period(s) in which land application did not occur, unless all previously accumulated sewage sludge has been removed and disposed of via a 
landfill, through incineration or by transfer to another treatment works.
- If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period, enter the results for the metal analysis in eDMR or on the 4500 
report and enter “0” for sludge weight and sludge fee weight.
- If no sewage sludge is removed from the facility during the reporting period and no metal analysis is completed during the reporting period, 
the permittee shall report under station 581 in the following manner:
- If metal analysis has not been completed previously during each reporting period: when sewage sludge is removed from the facility all metal 
analysis results shall be reported on the applicable DMR by entering the separate results on different days within the DMR. For example, if no 
sewage sludge has been removed from the facility for a full calendar year, and quarterly monitoring is required by the permit, then five (four 
from the previous year and one for the current monitoring period) separate composite samples of the sewage sludge are required to be 
collected and analyzed for metals prior to removal from the facility. The first sample result may be entered on the first day of the DMR, the 
second result on the second day of the DMR, and so on. A note may then be added to indicate the actual day(s) when the samples were 
collected.
- It is recommended that composite samples of the sewage sludge be collected and analyzed close enough to the time of land application to be 
reflective of the sludge’s current quality, but not so close that the results of the analysis are not available prior to land applying the sludge.
- The permittee shall maintain the appropriate records on site to verify that the requirements of Pathogen Reduction and Vector Attraction 
Reduction have been met.
- Sludge weight is a calculated total for the year. To convert from gallons of liquid sewage sludge to dry tons of sewage sludge: dry tons= 
gallons X 8.34 (Ibs/gallon) x 0.0005 (tons/lb) x decimal fraction total solids.

The permittee's pretreatment program, initially approved on May 9, 1985, and all

The permittee shall adopt and maintain legal authority which enables it to fully

identification and characterization of industrial sources, issuance of control documents, 
compliance monitoring and reporting, and enforcement.
The permittee shall establish agreements with all contributing jurisdictions, as necessary, 
to enable the permittee to fulfill its requirements wi± respect to industrial users 
discharging to its system.
The permittee shall identify all industrial users subject to pretreatment standards and 
requirements and characterize the nature and volume of pollutants in their wastewater.

within 30 days of making such a determination. This inventory shall be updated at a 
frequency to ensure proper identification and characterization of industrial users.
For the purpose of periodically reevaluating local limits, the permittee shall implement 
and maintain a sampling program to characterize pollutant contribution to the POTW 
from industrial and residential sources and to determine pollutant removal rates through 
the POTW. The permittee shall continue to review and develop local limits as necessary.

The permittee shall annually monitor priority pollutants, as defined by U.S. EPA, in the 
POTW's influent, effluent and sludge. Sample collection, preservation, and analysis shall 
be performed using U.S. EPA approved methods.
a. A sample of the influent and the effluent shall be collected when industrial discharges 
are occurring at normal to maximum levels. Sampling of the influent shall be done prior 
to any recycle streams and sampling of the effluent shall be after disinfection. Both 
samples shall be collected on the same day or, alternately, the effluent sample may be 
collected following the influent sample by approximately the retention time of the POTW.
b. A reasonable attempt shall be made to identify and quantify additional constituents 
(excluding priority pollutants and unsubstituted aliphatic compounds) at each sample 
location; Identification of additional peaks more than ten times higher than the adjacent 
background noise on the total ion plots (reconstructed gas chromatograms) shall be 
attempted through the use of U.S. EPA/NIH computerized library of mass spectra, with

Introduction
This Fact Sheet is prepared in order to document the technical basis and risk management decisions that are 
considered in the determination of water quality based NPDES Permit effluent limitations. The technical 
basis for the Fact Sheet may consist of evaluations of promulgated effluent guidelines, existing effluent 
quality, instream biological, chemical and physical conditions, and the relative risk of alternative effluent 
limitations. This Fact Sheet details the discretionary decision-making process empowered to the Director by 
the Clean Water Act and Ohio Water Pollution Control Law (ORC 6111). Decisions to award variances to 
Water Quality Standards or promulgated effluent guidelines for economic or technological reasons will also be 
justified in the Fact Sheet where necessary.
City of Urbana
205 South Main Street
Urbana, Ohio 43078
Development of a Fact Sheet for NPDES permits is mandated by Title 40 of the Code of Federal Regulations, 
Section 124.8 and 124.56. This document fulfills the requirements established in those regulations by 
providing the information necessary to inform the public of actions proposed by the Ohio Environmental 
Protection Agency, as well as the methods by which the public can participate in the process of finalizing 
those actions.
Effluent limits based on available treatment technologies are required by Section 301(b) of the Clean Water 
Act. Many of these have already been established by U.S. EPA in the effluent guideline regulations (a.k.a. 
categorical regulations) for industry categories in 40 CFR Parts 405^99. Technology-based regulations for 
publicly-owned treatment works are listed in the Secondary Treatment Regulations (40 CFR Part 133). If 
regulations have not been established for a category of dischargers, the director may establish technology­
based limits based on best professional judgment (BPJ).
Ohio EPA reviews the need for water-quality-based limits on a pollutant-by-pollutant basis. Wasteload 
allocations are used to develop these limits based on the pollutants that have been detected in the discharge, 
and the receiving water’s assimilative capacity. The assimilative capacity depends on the flow in the water 
receiving the discharge, and the concentration of the pollutant upstream. The greater the upstream flow, and 
the lower the upstream concentration, the greater the assimilative capacity is. Assimilative capacity may 
represent dilution (as in allocations for metals), or it may also incorporate the break-down of pollutants in the 
receiving water (as in allocations for oxygen-demanding materials).

Summary of Permit Conditions
The need for water-quality-based limits is determined by comparing the wasteload allocation for a pollutant to 
a measure of the effluent quality. The measure of effluent quality is called PEQ - Projected Effluent Quality. 
This is a statistical measure of the average and maximum effluent values for a pollutant. As with any 
statistical method, the more data that exists for a given pollutant, the more likely that PEQ will match the 
actual observed data. If there is a small data set for a given pollutant, the highest measured value is 
multiplied by a statistical factor to obtain a PEQ; for example if only one sample exists, the factor is 6.2, for 
two samples - 3.8, for three samples - 3.0. The factors continue to decline as samples sizes increase. These 
factors are intended to account for effluent variability, but if the pollutant concentrations are fairly constant, 
these factors may make PEQ appear larger than it would be shown to be if more sample results existed.
The effluent limits and monitoring requirements proposed for the following parameters are the same as in the 
current permit, although some monitoring frequencies might have changed: flow, temperature, dissolved 
oxygen, CBOD5, total suspended solids, ammonia-nitrogen, total phosphorus, nitrite-I-nitrate-nitrogen, oil and 
grease, total residual chlorine, pH, free cyanide, cadmium, total chromium, dissolved hexavalent chromium, 
copper, lead, mercury, nickel, zinc and total filterable residue (total dissolved solids).
Annual chronic toxicity testing with the determination of a acute endpoints is proposed for the life of the 
permit. Available data do not indicate that the plant’s effluent poses a toxicity problem, but federal NPDES 
application requirements at 40 CFR 122.21 require a permit holder to submit the results of four toxicity tests 
as part of its NPDES renewal application. The proposed monitoring will fulfill this requirement and 
adequately characterize toxicity in the plant’s effluent.
Final effluent limits are proposed for Escherichia coli. New water quality standards for E. coli\iec.?(ras. 
effective in March 2010.
New water-quality-based limits are proposed for silver. Effluent data show that it has reasonable potential to 
contribute to exceedances of water quality standards.
Because of nutrient-related impairment downstream in Great Miami River basin, monitoring is proposed for 
total Kjeldahl nitrogen.
The current monitoring requirement for heptachlor epoxide is being removed from the permit because data 
show that it does not pose an environmental hazard in the Urbana discharge.
In Part n of the permit, special conditions are included that address sanitary sewer overflow reporting; 
operator certification, minimum staffing and operator of record , outfall signage and the method detection 
limit used for silver analysis.

Facility Description
The City of Urbana has separate sanitary and storm sewers.
Description of Existing Discharge
Table 4 summarizes the results of acute and chronic whole effluent toxicity tests of the final effluent.
Use designations define the goals and expectations of a waterbody. These goals are set for aquatic life 
protection, recreation use and water supply use, and are defined in the Ohio WQS (OAC 3745-1-07). The use 
designations for individual waterbodies are listed in rules -08 through -32 of the Ohio WQS. Once the goals 
are set, numeric water quality standards are developed to protect these uses. Different uses have different 
water quality criteria.
The Urbana wastewater treatment plant has an average daily design flow of 3.0 MOD (million gallons per 
day). Wet stream processes are screening and grit removal, primary settling, trickling filtration, activated 
sludge - extended aeration, final clarification, chlorination, dechlorination and post aeration. Solid stream 
processes include aerobic digestion, dewatering using a belt filter press, microwave treatment, and disposal of 
stabilized sludge by land application at agronomic rates or hauling to a landfill
Use designations for aquatic life protection include habitats for coldwater fish and macroinvertebrates, 
warmwater aquatic life and waters with exceptional communities of warmwater organisms. These uses all 
meet the goals of the federal Clean Water Act. Ohio WQS also include aquatic life use designations for 
waterbodies which can not meet the Clean Water Act goals because of human-caused conditions that can not 
be remedied without causing fundamental changes to land use and widespread economic impact. The 
dredging and clearing of some small streams to support agricultural or urban drainage is the most common of 
these conditions. These streams are given Modified Warmwater or Limited Resource Water designations.
Recreation uses are defined by the depth of the waterbody and the potential for wading or swimming. Uses 
are defined for bathing waters, swimming/canoeing (Primary Contact) and wading only (Secondary Contact - 
generally waters too shallow for swimming or canoeing).
Water supply uses are defined by the actual or potential use of the waterbody. Public Water Supply 
designations apply near existing water intakes so that waters are safe to drink with standard treatment. Most 
other waters are designated for agricultural and industrial water supply.
Urbana implements an Ohio EPA- approved industrial pretreatment program. Based on information in their 
2010 NPDES renewal application, four categorical industrial users and one significant noncategorical 
industrial user discharge approximately 0.208 MOD to the wastewater plant.

Assessment of Impact on Receiving Waters
Three attainment status results are possible at each sampling location -full, partial, or non-attaiiunent. Full 
attainment means that all of the applicable indices meet the biocriteria. Partial attainment means that one or 
more of the applicable indices meet the biocriteria or one of the organism groups reflects poor or very poor 
performance. Nonattainment means that either none of the applicable indices meet the biocriteria or one of 
the organism groups indicates poor or very poor performance. An aquatic life use attainment table is 
constructed based on the sampling results and is arranged from upstream to downstream and includes the 
sampling locations indicated by river mile, the applicable biological indices, the use attainment status (i.e., 
full, partial, or non), the Qualitative Habitat Evaluation Index (QHEI), and comments and observations for 
each sampling location.
Under the provisions of 40 CFR 122.21(j), the Director has waived the requirement for submittal of expanded 
effluent testing data as part of the NPDES renewal application. Ohio EPA has access to substantially identical 
information through the submission of annual pretreatment program reports and/or from effluent testing 
conducted by the Agency.
An assessment of the impact of a permitted point source on the immediate receiving waters includes an 
evaluation of the available chemical/physical, biological, and habitat data which have been collected by Qhio 
EPA pursuant to the Five-Year Basin Approach for Monitoring and NPDES Reissuance. Other data may be 
used provided it was collected in accordance with Ohio EPA methods and protocols as specified by the Ohio 
Water Quality Standards and Ohio EPA guidance documents. Other information which may be evaluated 
includes, but is not limited to: NPDES permittee self-monitoring data; effluent and mixing zone bioassays 
conducted by Ohio EPA, the permittee, or U.S. EPA.
In evaluating this data, Ohio EPA attempts to link environmental stresses and measured pollutant exposure to 
the health and diversity of biological communities. Stresses can include pollutant discharges (permitted and 
unpermitted), land use effects, and habitat modifications. Indicators of exposure to these stresses include 
whole effluent toxicity tests, fish tissue chemical data, and fish health biomarkers (for example, fish blood 
tests).
Use attainment is a term which describes the degree to which environmental indicators are either above or 
below criteria specified by the Ohio Water Quality Standards (WQS; Ohio Administrative Code 3745-1). 
Assessing use attainment status for aquatic life uses primarily relies on the Ohio EPA biological criteria (OAC 
3745-1-07; Table 7-15). These criteria apply to rivers and streams outside of mixing zones. Numerical 
biological criteria are based on measuring several characteristics of the fish and macroinvertebrate 
communities; these characteristics are combined into multimetric biological indices including the Index of 
Biotic Integrity (EBI) and modified Index of Well-Being (Mlwb), which indicate the response of the fish 
community, and the Invertebrate Community Index (ICI), which indicates the response of the 
macroinvertebrate community. Numerical criteria are broken down by ecoregion, use designation, and stream 
or river size. Ohio has five ecoregions defined by common topography, land use, potential vegetation and 
soil type.
Ohio EPA conducted a biological and water quality survey of the Mad River basin in 2003. The results of 
that survey are included in the report Biological and Water Quality Study of the Mad River Basin, 2003 
(Ohio EPA; May 25, 2005), wWch is available through the following Ohio EPA web site: 
http://www.epa.ohio.gov/dsw/document index/psdindx.aspx .

Development of Water-Quality-Based Effluent Limits
Mad River is in full attainment of its Coldwater Habitat aquatic life use upstream and downstream of 
the Urbana wastewater treatment plant.
The 2003 study did identify areas of impairment in the Mad River basin caused by nutrients, habitat 
degradation and pathogen contamination. These impairments were addressed in the report Total 
Maximum Daily Loads for the Mad River Watershed (Final Report December 18, 2009 by Ohio EP A; 
approved by U.S. EPA January 26, 2010). TMDLs were calculated for nitrate, sedimentation, fecal 
coliform and habitat. The report did not make any recommendations for pollutant reductions or other 
actions at the Urbana wastewater treatment plant. The complete TMDL report is available at the 
following Ohio EPA web site:.http://epa.ohio.gov/Default.aspx?tabid=3563 .
The data were examined, and the following values were removed from the evaluation to give a more reliable 
projection of effluent quality: copper - one high value; mercury - one high value.
This data is evaluated statistically, and Projected Effluent Quality (PEQ) values are calculated for each 
pollutant. Average PEQ (PEQavg) values represent the 95“* percentile of monthly average data, and maximum 
PEQ (PEQmax) values represent the 95* percentile of all data points. The average and maximum PEQ values 
are presented in Table 3.
The PEQ values are used according to Ohio rules to compare to applicable water quality standards (WQS) and 
allowable wasteload allocation (WLA) values for each pollutant evaluated. Initially, PEQ values are 
compared to the applicable average and maximum WQS. If both PEQ values are less than 25 percent of the 
applicable WQS, the pollutant does not have the reasonable potential to cause or contribute to exceedances of 
WQS, and no wasteload allocation is done for that parameter. If either PEQavg or PEQmax is greater than 25 
percent of the applicable WQS, a wasteload allocation is conducted to determine whether the parameter 
exhibits reasonable potential and needs to have a limit or if monitoring is required. See Table 8 for a 
summary of the screening results.
Determining appropriate effluent concentrations is a multiple-step process in which parameters are identified 
as likely to be discharged by a facility, evaluated with respect to Ohio water quality criteria, and examined to 
determine the likelihood that the existing effluent could violate the calculated limits.

WasteloadAllocation For those parameters that require a WLA, the results are based on the uses assigned 
to the receiving waterbody in OAC 3745-1. Dischargers are allocated pollutant loadings/concentrations based 
on the Ohio Water Quality Standards (OAC 3745-1). Most pollutants are allocated by a mass-balance method 
because they do not degrade in the receiving water. Wasteload allocations using this method are done using 
the following general equation: Discharger WLA = (downstream flow x WQS) - (upstream flow x 
background concentration). Discharger WLAs are divided by the discharge flow so that the allocations are 
expressed as concentrations.

The proposed limit for total residual chlorine is based on wasteload allocation as limited by the inside mixing 
zone maximum (IMZM). The IMZM is a value calculated to avoid rapidly lethal conditions in the effluent

A continuation of monitoring for total phosphorus and nitrite+nitrate-nitrogen, plus new monitoring for total 
Kjeldahl nitrogen are proposed based on best engineering judgment. In addition, monitoring for total 
phosphorus and nitrite+nitrate-nitrogen is proposed at the upstream and downstream stations, 801 and 901. 
The Urbana wastewater plant discharges to the Mad River, which is part of the Great Miami River basin. 
The purpose of the monitoring is to maintain a data base on nutrient loadings and ambient concentrations in 
the basin. This data will be available for future studies addressing nutrient-related water quality impairment.
The Ohio EPA risk assessment (Table 8) places silver in group 5. This placement as well as the data in 
Tables 2 and 3 indicate that the reasonable potential to exceed WQS exists and limits are necessary to protect 
water quality. For this parameter, the PEQ is greater than 100 percent of the wasteload allocation. Pollutants 
that meet this requirement must have permit limits under OAC Rule 3745-33-07(A)(l).
Based on best engineering judgment, it is proposed that the existing permit limits for dissolved oxygen, total 
suspended solids, ammonia-nitrogen and 5-day carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (CBODs) be 
continued. The ammonia-nitrogen limits were reviewed and are protective of the water quality standard for 
ammonia toxicity.

The proposed silver limits are based on wasteload allocation (Table 7), and the monthly average limit, 0.51 
ug/1, is below the practical quantification level of 1.0 ug/1. Under paragraph (C) of Rule 3745-33-07, the 
permit will include a special condition in Part II stating the quantification level that will be used for assessing 
compliance with the limits.
To ensure that data is obtained that allows Ohio EPA to make water quality-related decisions regarding silver, 
a special condition is proposed in Part n of the permit that provides guidance on the MDL (method detection 
limit) the permittee should use in analyzing for this contaminant.
Heptachlor epoxide is included in group 5 under the risk assessment procedure (Table 8). However, based on 
best engineering judgment, limits or monitoring are not proposed for this pollutant. The preliminary effluent 
limit, 0.024 ug/1 (Table 7) is less than the method detection limits reported by Ohio EPA’s lab and most labs 
that perform analytical work for Ohio wastewater plants. The parent compound of this pollutant is a legacy 
pesticide that has been banned from general use, and monitoring would not yield data that is useable for 
making water quality-related decisions on heptachlor epoxide in the Urbana effluent.
Ohio EPA risk assessment (Table 8) places free cyanide, cadmium, total chromium, dissolved hexavalent 
chromium, copper, lead, nickel, zinc and total filterable residue (total dissolved solids) in groups 2 and 3. 
This placement as well as the data in Tables 2 and 3 support that these parameters do not have the reasonable 
potential to contribute to WQS exceedances, and limits are not necessary to protect water quality. Monitoring 
at a low frequency is proposed to document that these pollutants continue to remain at low levels.
Limits and monitoring requirements proposed for the disposal of sewage sludge by the following management 
practices are based on OAC 3745^0: land application, removal to sanitary landfill or transfer to another 
facility with an NPDES permit.
Additional monitoring requirements proposed at the final effluent, influent and upstream/downstream stations 
are included for all facilities in Ohio and vary according to the type and size of the discharge. In addition to 
permit compliance, this data is used to assist in the evaluation of effluent quality and treatment plant 
performance and for designing plant improvements and conducting future stream studies.
Whole Effluent Toxicity Reasonable Potential
Based on best engineering judgment, annual chronic toxicity testing with the determination of acute endpoints 
is proposed for the life of the permit. Evaluating the whole effluent toxicity data presented in Table 4 and 
other pertinent data under the provisions of OAC 3745-33-07(B) placed the Urbana wastewater plant in 
Category 4 with respect to whole effluent toxicity. While this indicates that the plant’s effluent does not 
currently pose a toxicity problem, federal NPDES application requirements at 40 CFR 122.21 require a 
permit holder to submit the results of four toxicity tests as part of its NPDES renewal application. The 
proposed monitoring will fulfill this requirement and adequately characterize toxicity in the plant’s effluent.
Ohio EPA risk assessment (Table 8) places mercury in group 4. This placement as well as the data in Tables 
2 and 3 support that this parameter does not have the reasonable potential to contribute to WQS exceedances, 
and limits are not necessary to protect water quality. Monitoring for Group 4 pollutants (where PEQ exceeds 
50 percent of the WLA) is required by OAC Rule 3745-33-07(A)(2).

Bis(2-ethylhexyl)phthalate and heptachlor epoxide are carcinogens, which requires the evaluation of the

equation must be included in the permit and used to determine compliance unless certain conditions

Other Requirements
For heptachlor epoxide, the average PEL, 0.024 ug/1, is less than the quantification level, 0.41 ug/1, so it can 
be removed from the additivity equation. As a result, it is not necessary to include the additivity equation in 
the permit.
Storm Water Compliance
To comply with industrial storm water regulations, the permittee submitted a form for "No Exposure 
Certification", and the Agency issued the certification on December 29, 2010. Compliance with the industrial 
storm water regulations must be re-affirmed every five years. No later than December 29, 2015, the permittee 
must submit a new form for "No Exposure Certification" or make other provisions to comply with the 
industrial storm water regulations.
Schedule of Compliance
A six month compliance schedule is proposed for the City to submit a technical justification for either revising 
its local industrial user limits or retaining its existing local limits. If revisions to local limits are required, the 
City must also submit a pretreatment program modification request.
A six month compliance schedule is proposed for the City to submit a pretreatment program modification 
request for implementing changes required by Ohio’s pretreatment rules and U.S. EPA ‘s pretreatment 
streamlining rule.
Sanitary Sewer Overflow Reporting
Provisions for reporting sanitary sewer overflows (SSOs) are also proposed in this permit. These provisions 
include: the reporting of the system-wide number of SSO occurrences on monthly operating reports; telephone 
notification of Ohio EPA and the local health department, and 5-day follow up written reports for certain high 
risk SSOs; and preparation of an annual report that is submitted to Ohio EPA and made available to the 
public. Many of these provisions were already required under the “Noncompliance Notification”, “Records 
Retention”, and “Facility Operation and Quality Control” general conditions in Part HI of Ohio NPDES 
permits.
Operator Certification
Operator certification requirements have been included in Part II, Item A of the permit in accordance with 
rules adopted in December 2006. These rules require that the City of Urbana have a Class HI wastewater 
treatment plant operator in charge of the sewage treatment plant operations discharging through outfall 001.
Operator of Record
In December 2006, Ohio Administrative Code rule revisions became effective that affect the requirements for 
certified operators for sewage collection systems and treatment works regulated under NPDES permits. Part 
n. Item A of this NPDES permit is included to implement rule 3745-7-02 of the Ohio Administrative Code 
(OAC). It requires the permittee to designate one or more operator of record to oversee the technical 
operation of the treatment works.
Outfall Signage
Part n of the permit includes requirements for the permittee to place a sign at each outfall to the Mad River 
providing information about the discharge. Signage at outfalls is required pursuant to Ohio Administrative 
Code 3745-33-08(A).

Comments
The Mad Rrver/Nettle Creek Assessment Unit includes the Mad River and tributaries downstream from Kings Cr, 
(RM 43.8) to downstream from Chapman Cr. (RM 32.6). Biological and habitat assessments were conducted at 31 
sites in 2003 ranging in drainage area between 0.6 mi^ and 264 mi'. Twenty-three sites within the assessment unit 
have been designated or are recommended for a CWH aquatic life use. Nineteen sites were in full attainment of the 
CWTI use. Three sites supported biological communities that partially attained ecoregional expectations and one 
site, Stoney Creek, was in nonattainment of the CWH use. Eight sites within the assessment unit have been 
designated or recommended for W’WH aquatic life use. Five sites w’ere in full attainment of the WWTI use. Dugan 
Run partially met WWH biocriteria and two sites on the St. Paris tributary to Nettle Creek were not attaining the 
use. One site, Russell Creek, went dry before sanqiling could be completed. The AVAU overall attainment score was 
89.5.
The PCR use designation was not attained in this assessment unit based on the ten sites sampled for fecal coliform 
and E. coli. The highest median concentrations in die assessment unit occurred in the St. Paris tributary at RM 2.66 
iqjstream from die St. Paris WWTP discharge. Elev'ated bacteria concentrations throughout the survey area 
generally occurred after precipitation.
The high WAU overall attainment score reflects the majority of sites meeting aquatic life use designations. The 
mainstem reach of die Mad River supported health}’ fish and macroinvertebrate communities. Impairments were 
documented in several tributaries. Most noticeable was die degraded condition of the St Paris tributary to Nettle 
Creek which resulted from organic and nutrient loading from die WWTP and an improperly functioning SSO. 
Other sources of impairment, included urban runoff from Urbana into Dugan Run and enrichment and habitat 
limitations associated with agricultural practices in the watershed.
Summary of Mad River assessment unit scoring. The assessment unit score is an average grade of 
aquatic life use status. An assessment unit score of 80 is used as the benchmark above which a watershed 
in considered to be in good condition relative to aquatic life uses. A maximum assessment unit score of 
100 is possible if all monitored sites meet designated aquatic life uses. The method of calculation is 
presented in the 2002 Integrated Water Quality Monitoring and Assessment Report 
(www.epa.state.ohus/dsw’/taidl/2002IntReport/20020hioIntegtatedRepQtt.html). The comments 
provided include principal causes and sources of impact on aquatic life and recreational uses and 
significant contaminants in sediment and fish tissue.

- For the purpose of counting occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of

6. Industrial Compliance Monitoring

The permittee shall sample and inspect industrial users in accordance with the approved 
program or approved modifications, including inspection and sampling of all significant 
industrial users at least annually. Sample collection, preservation and analysis must be

produce evidence admissible injudicial enforcement proceedings.
The permittee shall also require, receive, and review self-monitoring and other industrial

user’s self-monitoring, the permittee shall perform repeat sampling and analysis within 30 
days of becoming aware of a permit violation, unless the permittee notifies the user of the 
violation and requires the user to perform the repeat analysis and reporting.
The permittee shall annually monitor priority pollutants, as defined by U.S. EPA, in the 
POTW's influent, effluent and sludge. Sample collection, preservation, and analysis shall 
be performed using U.S. EPA approved methods.
a. A sample of the influent and the effluent shaU be collected when industrial discharges 
are occmring at normal to maximum levels. Sampling of the influent shall be done prior 
to any recycle streams and sampling of the effluent shall be after disinfection. Both 
samples shall be collected on the same day or, alternately, the effluent sample may be 
collected following the influent sample by approximately the retention time of the POTW.
Sampling of sludge shall be representative of sludge removed to final disposal. A 
minimum of one grab sample shall be taken during actual sludge removal and disposal 
unless the POTW uses more than one disposal option. If multiple disposal options are 
used, the POTW shall collect a composite of grab samples from all disposal practices 
which are proportional to the annual flows to each type of disposal.
b. A reasonable attempt shall be made to identify and quantify additional constituents 
(excluding priority pollutants and unsubstituted aliphatic compounds) at each sample 
location. Identification of additional peaks more than ten times higher than the adjacent 
background noise on the total ion plots (reconstructed gas chromatograms) shall be 
attempted through the use of U.S. EPA/NIH computerized library of mass spectra, with 
visual confirmation by an experienced analyst. Quantification may be based on an order 
of magnitude estimate compared with an internal standard.
The results of these samples must be submitted on Ohio EPA Form 4221 with the

Sanitary sewer overflows that enter waters of the state, either directly or through a storm 
sewer or other conveyance, shall be reported on your monthly operating reports. You 
must report the system-wide number of occurrences for SSOs that enter waters of the 
state in accordance with the requirements for station number 300. A monitoring table for 
this station is included in Part 1, B of this NPDES permit. For the purpose of counting 
occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an overflow, spill, 
release, or diversion of wastewater on a given day is counted as one occurrence. For 
example, if on a given day overflows occur from a manhole at one location and from a 
damaged pipe at another location and they both enter waters of the state, you should 
record two occurrences for that day. If overflows from both locations continue on the 
following day, you should record two occurrences for the following day. At the end of 
the month, total the daily occurrences from all locations on your system and report this 
number using reporting code 74062 (Overflow Occurrence, No./Month) on the 4500 form 
for station number 300.

City of Urbana
1.0 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Page 1 of 54
Master Plan
Water Pollution Control Facility
The City of Urbana, Ohio currently operates a 3 Million Gallon per Day (MGD) trickling 
filter/solids contact activated sludge Water Pollution Control Facility (WPCF). The 
current plant v/as constructed in 1975 with process improvements (chlorination/de- 
chlorination and post aeration) added in 1990. Improvements are needed to address a 
variety of deficiencies at the WPCF.
This 20 year Master Plan was developed to help in the evaluation, scheduling and 
coordination of the improvements. The Master Plan integrates the various needs into 
one focused capital improvement plan. A master plan is a requirement of the Ohio 
EPA and other state and federal agencies to qualify for low interest State Revolving 
Fund financing for wastewater improvements.
The 2008 average daily flow for the plant was at 2.18 MGD or 75 % of design flow. The 
peak flows recorded at the plant exceed the peak design flows. Due to the recent 
downturn in the economy population and growth projections for the area are probably 
not reliable; however, if another industry such as Fox Paper would want to begin 
operations in Urbana the wastewater from such an operation would put the plant at 
full capacity.
In addition to nearing its treatment capacity, the plant has outdated processes that 
require unusual amounts of operational attention to ensure no solids discharge 
violations. The plant has also experienced several problems with major pieces of 
equipment breaking down. Compounding the concerns with equipment reliability is 
the sensitive nature of the receiving stream. Mad River. Given these circumstances, 
upgrading the wastewater treatment plant to address capacity concerns and 
equipment replacement needs is vital to the continued growth of the community and 
the protection of the Mad River. Timing of these improvements is also important. If 
design on the selected plan is started this summer, the new facilities would most 
likely not be operational until fall 2015. At that point, it is very likely that the 
wastewater flows and loads would already have exceeded the current facilities design 
capacity.
To address these deficiencies and best meet the needs of the City over the planning 
period, four main alternatives were identified for expanding the capacity of the 
plant. These include; 1-expanding the current TF/SC process, 2-converting the 
aeration tanks to Integrated Fixed Film Activated Sludge tanks, 3-constructing a 
parallel oxidation ditch plant to treat half the flow, and 4-constructing a parallel 
membrane bioreactor (MIBR) plant to treat half the flow.
Alternates 1 and 2 require increasing the capacity of the existing underground pipes 
and tanks which would be very difficult and costly while keeping the plant in

Alternate 3 is the lowest capital (and O&M) cost option. The oxidation ditch would 
meet the needs of the City and provide a high quality effluent with reasonable 
operation requirements. The oxidation ditch process has had improvements in 
technology that allow it to be automatic with real time monitoring. The process is 
proven and very reliable. Alternate 3 is $2,000,000.00 less expensive than any of the 
other options and because of these reasons WSA recommends to the City that the 
oxidation ditch process be used to upgrade the WPCF. Should the City, due to the 
environmental sensitivity of the receiving stream, want to provide an even higher 
level of treatment than what the Ohio EPA and current standards require then 
Alternate 4 provides the highest level of treatment and highest quality effluent.

Enclosed is the report of the biomonitoring on the sample listed above. The objective of the 
chronic biomonitoring was to determine the effects, both the acute endpoint (mortality) and 
chronic endpoints (mortality and growth, or reproduction), from the test water. Fathead minnow 
larvae (Pimephalespromelas) were the test organisms.
Acute toxicity was determined by locating the median lethal concentration (LC50) and the 
median effective concentration (EC50). Growth was determined from the dry weight of surviving 
Pimephales promelas larvae.
Alloway (Lima, Ohio) performs biomonitoring testing in accordance with procedures established 
by the Environmental Protection Agency. The Standard Operating Procedures for the testing is 
on file with the Ohio EPA.
Dissolved oxygen, pH, and temperature were recorded daily at each renewal and at the end of 
each 24-hour exposure period. Results may be found in Appendix C "Parameter Data Sheets". 
Samples were analyzed for alkalinity, hardness and conductivity. These results may also be 
found in Appendix C.

- A sanitary sewer overflow is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater from a sanitary sewer system. These overflows shall be 
monitored when they discharge.
- For the purpose of counting occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of 
wastewater on a given day that enters waters of the state is counted as one occurrence. For example, if on a given day overflows occur from a 
manhole at one location and from a damaged pipe at another location and they both enter waters of the state, record two occurrences for that 
day. If overflows from both locations continue on the following day, record two occurrences for the following day. At the end of the month, 
total the daily occurrences and report this number in the first column of the first day of the month on the 4500 form. If there are no overflows 
during the entire month, report "zero" (0).
- All sanitary sewer overflows are prohibited except under emergency conditions where the overflow occurs in full compliance with all of the 
provisions of 40 CFR 122.41(m) and Part HI Item 11 of this NPDES permit.

PART in - GENERAL CONDITIONS
1. DEFINITIONS
"Daily discharge" means the discharge of a pollutant measured during a calendar day or any 24-hour 
period that reasonably represents the calendar day for purposes of sampling. For pollutants with 
limitations expressed in units of mass, the "daily discharge" is calculated as the total mass of the pollutant 
discharged over the day. For pollutants with limitations expressed in other units of measurement, the 
"daily discharge" is calculated as the average measurement of the pollutant over the day.
"Average weekly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar week, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar week divided 
by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that week. Each of the following 7-day periods is 
defined as a calendar week: Week 1 is Days 1 - 7 of the month; Week 2 is Days 8-14; Week 3 is Days 
15-21; and Week 4 is Days 22 - 28. If the "daily discharge" on days 29, 30 or 31 exceeds the "average 
weekly" discharge limitation, Ohio EPA may elect to evaluate the last 7 days of the month as Week 4 
instead of Days 22 - 28. Compliance with fecal coliform bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be 
determined using the geometric mean.
"Average monthly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar month, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar month 
divided by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that month. Compliance with fecal 
coliform bacteria or E coli bacteria limitations shall be determined using the geometric mean.
"85 percent removal" means the arithmetic mean of the values for effluent samples collected in a period 
of 30 consecutive days shall not exceed 15 percent of the arithmetic mean of the values for influent 
samples collected at approximately the same times during the same period.
"Net concentration" shall mean the difference between the concentration of a given substance in a sample 
taken of the discharge and the concentration of the same substances in a sample taken at the intake which 
supplies water to the given process. For the purpose of this definition, samples that are taken to 
determine the net concentration shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six 
increments taken at regular intervals throughout the plant day.

"Absolute Limitations" Compliance with limitations having descriptions of "shall not be less than," "nor 
greater than," "shall not exceed," "minimum," or "maximum" shall be determined from any single value 
for effluent samples and/or measurements collected.

text:
Outfall Signage
Monitoring Report Name Change
Not later than 4 months from the effective date of this permit, the permittee shall post a 
permanent marker on the stream hank at each outfall that is regulated under this NPDES 
permit where a marker does not currently exist. This includes final outfalls, bypasses, and 
combined sewer overflows. The marker shall consist at a minimum of the name of the 
establishment to which the permit was issued, the Ohio EPA permit number, and the 
outfall number and a contact telephone number. The information shall be printed in letters 
not less than two inches in height. The marker shall be a minimum of 2 feet by 2 feet and 
shall be a minimum of 3 feet above ground level. The sign shall not be obstructed such 
that persons in boats or persons swimming on the river or someone fishing or walking 
along the shore cannot read the sign. Vegetation shall be periodically removed to keep the 
sign visible. If the outfall is normally submerged the sign shall indicate that. If the outfall 
is a combined sewer outfall, the sign shall indicate that untreated human sewage may be 
discharged from the outfall during wet weather and that harmful bacteria may be present

Subject: Ohio Environmental Protection Agency NPDES Inspection  
 
Dear Mr. Herrman: 
 
Thank you for accompanying me during Ohio EPA's August 13, 2025, compliance evaluation 
inspection of the City of Urbana’s Water Pollution Control Facility. Along with myself, Glen 
Vonderembse, Madeline Mason, and Jared Szwec from the Ohio EPA's SWDO District Office, 
were also present during the inspection. 
  
The purpose of the inspection was to evaluate compliance with the terms and conditions of 
your National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit and to evaluate the 
operation and maintenance of the plant. 
The City of Urbana’s Water Pollution Control Facility liquid treatment process consists of (3) 
influent screw pumps, fine screening, grit and grease removal, (2) oxidation ditches, (4) 
secondary clarifiers, tertiary filtration, ultraviolet disinfection, and post aeration.  The final 
effluent is discharged into the Mad River.  The facility also utilizes (2) sludge digesters and has 
a screened septage equalization basin for septage receiving.

Dear Mr. Hall: 
 
On September 9, 2025 I conducted a Pretreatment Compliance Inspection (PCI) of the city of 
Urbana’s (City) Pretreatment Program. Zac Herrmann and Mark Mabry represented the 
facility during the inspection. The cooperation provided during the inspection is much 
appreciated. 
The purpose of the inspection was to evaluate compliance with the requirements of the City’s 
approved Pretreatment Program. The PCI followed a checklist designed by Ohio EPA to 
evaluate all aspects of the City’s Pretreatment Program. There was one violation identified 
during the inspection addressed in a separate Notice of Violation (NOV) letter. In addition, a 
discussion of observations along with recommended actions is provided below. 
Findings: 
1. The City failed to submit the Quarterly Industrial User Violation Report (QIUVR) for the 
fourth quarter of calendar year 2024 in a timely manner. 
 
2. The industrial user (IU) permit the City issued to Weidman Electrical Technology does 
not include the required sample type for the categorical standards applied.

title: 3858475.pdf
text:
Page 2 of 3 
 
 
 
 
3. The City has identified Weidmann Electrical Technology as subject to categorical 
standards at 40 CFR 430.117 (PSNS) but has not identified the type of facility covered 
under Subpart K of that category. Additionally, the City was unable to demonstrate 
how the production-based standards of the category and included in the IU permit 
were calculated. 
 
4. The City appears to be accepting self-monitoring reporting forms from Weidmann 
Electrical Technology that include certification language for reporting on parameters 
associated with monitoring for surcharge purposes. However, the City only appears to 
be accepting laboratory analytical reports from Weidmann Electrical Technology for 
self-monitoring of parameters associated with categorical standards.  
 
Recommendations: 
The recommendation(s) are offered by Ohio EPA in an effort to provide compliance assistance 
to your facility. 
1. The matter regarding the QIUVR not being submitted in a timely manner will be 
addressed in a separate Notice of Violation (NOV) letter. 
 
2. The City should ensure the sampling type is clearly included in IU permits for all 
parameters in which monitoring is required. 
 
3. The City should maintain documentation demonstrating how the categorical limits 
included in the permit are calculated. If Weidmann Electrical Technology is not using 
chlorophenolic-containing biocides, the IU must provide certification that it is not 
using these biocides. 
 
4. IU self-monitoring reports require certification as outlined by OAC 3745-03-06(F). Self-
monitoring reporting forms should be updated to include certification language and 
the City should ensure all self-monitoring reports received are signed and certified in 
accordance with OAC 3745-03-06(F).

Subject: Notice of Violation / Resolution of Violation - Significant Non-Compliance

Dear Mr. Hall: 
 
Ohio EPA, Division of Surface Water (DSW), conducted a Pretreatment Compliance Inspection (PCI) of 
the city of Urbana (Urbana) pretreatment program September 9, 2025. As discussed during the site 
visit, the goal of the inspection was to determine Urbana’s compliance with Ohio's environmental 
laws and regulations found in Chapter 6111 of the Ohio Revised Code (ORC) and Chapter 3745-3 of 
the Ohio Administrative Code (OAC) and the terms and conditions of the Urbana Wastewater 
Treatment Plants (WWTP) National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits 
1PD00011 issued on October 26, 2020. The inspection included a review of operations and written 
documentation associated with pretreatment program implementation. An inspection report is 
provided under separate cover. 
 
Violations 
 
Ohio EPA DSW observed the following violation of Ohio’s environmental laws and regulations and 
Urbana’s permit terms and conditions. It is recommended you promptly address the violation. 
 
1. Violation Description: Urbana failed to submit the Quarterly Industrial User Violation 
Report 
(QIUVR) for the fourth quarter of calendar year 2024 in a timely manner. This is a violation of ORC 
6111.07(A), OAC 3745-3-03(C), and Part II.W.10. of Urbana’s permit.

title: 3858492.pdf
text:
Page 2 of 3 
 
 
 
 
Additional Information: Please be advised that the violation cited is considered a Level I 
Reportable Non-compliance violation due to the failure to submit a pretreatment report to Ohio 
EPA DSW within 30 days of the due date specified in the NPDES permit. Due to Urbana having a 
violation meeting the Level I criterion for Reportable Non-compliance, Urbana is now being 
categorized as being in Significant Non-Compliance (SNC). 
 
Requested Action: Please submit the fourth quarter 2024 QIUVR at the earliest opportunity. 
 
Resolution: On 9/30/2025 Ohio EPA DSW received Urbana’s completed fourth quarter 2024 
QIUVR electronically through the eBusiness center. Therefore, this violation has been resolved  
  
Conclusion  
 
Within 30 days of receipt of this letter, please provide documentation to Ohio EPA DSW of the 
actions taken and/or will be taken to resolve the violations cited above. Documentation of steps 
taken to resolve these violations includes but is not limited to: written correspondence, updated 
policies, and photographs, as appropriate, and may be submitted via the postal service or 
electronically to Tyler.Bowman@epa.ohio.gov. If circumstances delay resolution of violations, 
Urbana is requested to contact Ohio EPA DSW to discuss the situation and propose an alternative 
schedule to resolve the violations in a timely manner. 
 
Failure to comply with Chapter 6111 of the Ohio Revised Code and rules promulgated thereunder 
may result in an administrative or civil penalty. 
 
Please note that the submission of any requested information to respond to this letter does not 
constitute waiver of the Ohio EPA’s authority to seek administrative or civil penalties as provided in 
Chapter 6111.09 of the Ohio Revised Code.   
 
Should you have any questions, please contact me at 937.285.6475 and/or 
Tyler.Bowman@epa.ohio.gov. 
 
Sincerely,

Subject: Ohio Environmental Protection Agency NPDES Municipal Stormwater Notice of

Dear Mr. Hall: 
 
Ohio EPA, Division of Surface Water (DSW), conducted a audit of the City of Urbana’s (the City) 
Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) program on December 17, 2025. The 
inspection focused on the implementation requirements for  all Minimum Control Measures 
(MCM), #1 and #2 “Public Education and Public Involvement and Participation”, #3 “Illicit 
Discharge Detection and Elimination”, #4 and #5 “Construction & Post-Construction Programs” 
and #6 “Pollution Prevention and Good Housekeeping”.  Chad Hall; Public Works, Zac 
Hermann; Wastewater and Tyler Bumbalough; Engineering represented the City of Urbana, and 
I represented Ohio EPA, Division of Surface Water. The goal of the inspection was to determine 
Urbana’s compliance with Ohio’s environmental laws and regulations as found in Ohio Revised 
Code (ORC) Chapter 6111, Ohio Administrative Code (OAC) Chapter 3745-39, and the terms 
and conditions of Ohio EPA’s National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) small 
MS4 General Permit. Urbana most recently renewed NPDES Small MS4 general permit 
coverage on December 6, 2021. The City of Urbana originally obtained coverage on June 5, 
2009. 
Our inspection included a review of the City’s Stormwater Management Program (SWMP), the 
City’s 2023 and 2024 annual reports and MS4 program records. The inspection also included an 
inspection of the City’s Service Facility to evaluate the good housekeeping practices of the 
facility. 
Detailed findings and recommendations can be found in Ohio EPA’s MS4 inspection 
Worksheets, which will accompany this letter.

title: 3959035.pdf
text:
Violations 
 
Ohio EPA DSW observed the following violations of Ohio’s environmental laws and regulations. 
It is recommended you promptly address these violations. 
1. Violation Description: The City of Urbana has not updated their SWMP to meet the 
conditions of the current MS4 permit. This is a violation of ORC 6111.07(A), and Part 
III.A.2. of the OHQ000004 permit. 
Additional Information: The City of Urbana initially developed a SWMP in 2007 and 
updated it in 2021. The SWMP was not amended to ensure compliance with changes 
and additions to all permit requirements. 
Additional Information: When issuing MS4 Permit OHQ000004, Ohio EPA amended 
Part I.B.3.b which establishes authorized non-storm water discharges to the MS4. The 
City of Urbana has not updated their SWMP to incorporate these changes.  
Requested Action: Please provide a written plan of corrective action to address this 
violation. You should update the SWMP to ensure compliance with MS4 Permit 
OHQ000004 and issues raised in the Additional Information above. To demonstrate 
compliance, please submit a copy of the updated SWMP, including your updated 
ordinance. 
2. Violation Description: The City of Urbana has not updated their Storm Sewer System 
Map to meet the conditions of the current MS4 permit. This is a violation of ORC 
6111.07(A), and Part III.B.3.b of the OHQ000004 permit. 
Additional Information: When issuing MS4 Permit OHQ000004, Ohio EPA established 
that the City’s comprehensive storm sewer system map shall also include the City’s 
small MS4 system (owned and/or operated by Urbana), including catch basins, pipes, 
ditches, flood control facilities (retention/detention ponds), post-construction water 
quality BMPs (public and private) which have been installed to satisfy Ohio EPA’s 
NPDES Construction Stormwater General Permit and/or your local post-construction 
water quality BMP requirements. 
Additional Information: Post-construction BMPs shall be identified by type of practice 
(e.g., wet extended detection basin, bioretention, etc.). Previously existing post-
construction BMPs shall be identified by type of practice within five (5) years of the 
effective date of permit OHQ000004. 
Requested Action: Please update the City’s Storm Sewer System Map to include all 
Publicly and Privately owned post-construction BMP’s that have been installed within the 
city since this permit went into effect.  
3. Violation Description: The City of Urbana does not use an objective tool such as 
software or checklist to document each SWP3 review. This is a violation of 
ORC6111.07(A), and Part III.B.4.c.ii of the OHQ000004 permit.

title: 3959035.pdf
text:
6. Violation Description: The City of Urbana practices improper disposal methods for 
roadkill by burying roadkill on City owned property. This is a violation of ORC 
6111.07(A), and Part III.B.6.d.iii.3 of the OHQ000004 permit. 
Additional Informal: Procedures for the proper management and disposal of waste 
removed from your small MS4 and your municipal operations, including dredge spoil, 
accumulated sediments, floatables, street sweepings/catch basin cleanings and other 
debris. 
Additional Information: The practice of removing animal carcasses from roadways is 
essential to public safety.  As a safety measure, it is acceptable for road crews to 
merely remove an animal carcass from the roadway and place the dead animal in an 
adjacent public right-of-way. The carcass should not be placed in a ditch or other 
location in which it can become submerged in water, or in a manner that contributes to 
pollution of waterways. In addition, the carcass should not be placed near farm animals 
grazing areas. Whenever possible, cover the carcass with a minimum of six (6) inches of 
wood chips. Please be aware that onsite burials would be considered open dumping or 
operating an illegal landfill. Some municipalities, counties and government agencies 
have established composting facilities to compost the dead animals they collect. This 
option typically requires establishing a Class III composting facility. 
Requested Action: Please provide a written plan of corrective action to address this 
violation. If interested in establishing a composting facility for the purpose of managing 
dead animals, contact the Ohio EPA Division of Materials and Waste Management.  
7. Violation Description: The City of Urbana does not have a SWPPP for the composting 
facility. . This is a violation of ORC 6111.07(A), and Part III.B.6.c of the OHQ000004 
permit. 
Additional Information: For your municipal facilities that conduct activities described in 
40 CFR 122.26(b)(14) that are not required to obtain Industrial Storm Water General 
Permit coverage, including vehicle maintenance facilities, bus terminals, composting 
facilities, impoundment lots and waste transfer stations, a Storm Water Pollution 
Prevention Plan (SWPPP) shall be developed and implemented in accordance with the 
SWP3 requirements of OHR000006. 
Requested Action: Please provide a written plan of corrective action to address this 
violation to develop a SWPPP for the Composting Facility that the City operates. 
 
Conclusion   
  
Within 30 days of receipt of this letter, please provide documentation to Ohio EPA DSW of the 
actions taken and/or will be taken to resolve the violations cited above. Documentation of steps 
taken to resolve this (these) violation(s) includes but is not limited to: writ ten correspondence, 
updated policies, and photographs, as appropriate, and may be submitted via the postal service 
or electronically to Daniel.hoit@epa.ohio.gov.  If circumstances delay resolution of violations, The 
City of Urbana is requested to contact Ohio EPA DSW to discuss the situation and propose an 
alternative schedule to resolve the violations in a timely manner.

Coordination with Ohio EPA’s NPDES Permit Program 
The community should verify NOI submittal to Ohio EPA as part of the SWP3 review process 
and certainly by the pre-construction meeting.  When the community discovers that an NOI 
has not been submitted after construction activities begin, it should notify Ohio EPA with the 
name of the development, operator contact information and date that construction activities 
commenced.  Both the primary operator (developer) and day-to-day site operator (contractor

title: 3959035.pdf
text:
or construction management company) require permit coverage.  The primary operator 
should have submitted the NOI and the secondary operator(s) a Co-Permittee NOI. 
 
When parcels within a subdivision are sold to a different operator, the new operator (typically 
a homebuilding company) is to submit an Individual Lot NOI.  Submittal of the Individual Lot 
NOI should be verified by the Village. 
 
Ohio EPA maintains a publicly-accessible database of NOIs, Co-Permittee NOIs and 
Individual Lot NOIs that is updated daily.  This information can be found at 
https://epa.ohio.gov/dsw/permits/gplist. 
 
When construction activities are completed, permanent (post-construction) storm water 
management practices have been installed and areas disturbed by construction have been 
permanently stabilized, the community should advise site operators to submit Notices of 
Termination (NOTs).  This will remove the NPDES permit from the active list. 
 
Post-Construction BMP Implementation Review 
Ohio EPA and the community reviewed the implementation of post-construction BMPs on 
some construction sites that have been completed and that obtained NPDES permit coverage

NOTES 
Site Inspection for SWP3 Implementation 
The SWMP should include a standardized construction site inspection checklist that is to be 
utilized by construction site inspectors to document SWP3 implementation.  You may develop 
your own to ensure compliance with local standards or adopt/modify the Ohio EPA 
construction site inspection checklist available online under the Construction Activities tab at 
www.epa.ohio.gov/dsw/storm/index.aspx.  After clicking on the “Construction Activities” tab, 
click on the “Information and Permit Compliance Materials” tab. 
 
Deficiencies and violations noted in the inspection reports are to be communicated by the 
community to the site operator(s) and the community is to establish a deadline for corrective 
action per the enforcement escalation plan. 
 
Verification of Post-Construction BMP Installation 
Final site inspection should include verification that permanent (post-construction) BMPs have 
been constructed per the approved SWP3.  Some communities require the submittal of an as-
built drawing to verify installation.  However, active inspection during the construction process 
is recommended, particularly for green infrastructure such as bioretention.  In addition to the 
specifications in the SWP3, guidance on the construction of post-construction BMPs can be 
found in Chapter 2 of Ohio EPA’s Rainwater and Land Development manual available 
online at https://epa.ohio.gov/dsw/storm/technical_guidance.   
 
Ohio EPA requires that the SWP3 include a long-term maintenance plan for post-construction 
BMPs.  This is to be a stand-alone document containing the following information:  (1) a 
designated entity for storm water inspection and maintenance responsibilities, (2) the routine 
and non-routine maintenance tasks to be undertaken, (3) a schedule for inspection and 
maintenance, (4) any necessary legally-binding maintenance easements and agreements, (5) 
construction drawings or excerpts showing the plan view, profile view and details of the 
outlet(s), (6) a map showing all access and maintenance easements, and (7) relevant 
elevations and associated volumes that dictate when removal of accumulated sediments 
must occur.  The Village should include these minimum requirements in local requirements 
and ensure that the entity responsible to conduct long-term maintenance activities is given a 
copy of the long-term maintenance plan from the approved SWP3.

Long-Term Maintenance of Post-Construction BMPs 
Once post-construction BMPs are installed, the community is required to enact a program to 
ensure their long-term maintenance.  To develop an inventory of these practices, Part 
III.B.3.b of the NPDES permit requires that they be added to the comprehensive MS4 map.  
Although some communities take operational responsibility for post-construction BMPs, most 
communities rely on the property owner or homeowners’ associations (HOAs) to conduct 
long-term maintenance activities.  Still, the community must ensure that long-term 
maintenance is occurring. 
 
To that end, Ohio EPA recommends a program that uses both self-inspection by the property 
owner or HOA and active inspection by the community (e.g., self-inspection annually with 
community verification at least once per 5-year NPDES permit term).  The community should 
consider developing a checklist or report form to be utilized by the property owner or HOA 
when conducting long-term maintenance inspections and should distribute educational 
materials to property owners and HOAs on proper long-term maintenance of post-
construction BMPs.  The Village may want to establish minimum qualifications for BMP 
inspectors in local ordinance to ensure that a knowledgeable person is conducting the self-
inspections.  Guidance on the long-term maintenance of post-construction BMPs is available 
in the Rainwater and Land Development manual or the Maintaining Storm Water Control 
Measures manual available from the NE Ohio Storm Water Training Council website at 
www.neohiostormwater.com.
